articles.title: The Heirs Who Never Met Him
articles.dek: An Iowa carpenter left his life savings to strangers he would never see. Hebrews says Jesus left a will too, and his has one detail no other will in history has ever had.
articles.quote: Every other will is read after the giver is gone; this one is carried out by the Giver himself, alive, who has promised to come and see his heirs face to face.
articles.body:
For nearly seven decades, Dale Schroeder went to work at the same company in Iowa as a carpenter, building and repairing things with his hands. He never married and never had children. Friends remembered that he owned two pairs of jeans, one for work and one for church, and that he drove an old Chevy pickup long after most people would have replaced it. Nobody in his small town thought of him as a rich man. Then, not long before he died in 2005, he sat down with his lawyer, Steve Nielsen, and explained what he wanted done with the money he had quietly saved. Dale had never gone to college, and he wanted to help small-town Iowa kids who could not afford to go. When the lawyer asked how much there was, the answer was close to three million dollars.

Over the years that followed, the fund paid for the education of thirty-three young people, many of them the first in their families to earn a degree. They became teachers, nurses, therapists and counselors. In 2019, when the money had finally been spent, the recipients gathered to honor the carpenter, and their story traveled around the world. Reporters called them "Dale's Kids," even though not one of them had ever met him. The only thing he asked in return was that they pass the kindness on to someone else someday.

Filipinos understand the weight of a will. In Tagalog the word for inheritance is mana, and every family knows the hush that falls when a parent is gone and the papers are finally opened. Sometimes a will brings peace and sometimes it starts a quarrel over a piece of land, yet it always carries the same ache, because the gift arrives only after the giver has died. In Hebrews 9, the writer tells us that Jesus also left a will, and that he named us in it.

Hebrews was written to Jewish Christians who were weary and under pressure, tempted to drift back to the familiar world of the temple, its priests and its sacrifices. Chapter 9 sets the old system beside the new one. To feel its force, you have to stand where those first readers stood in their memories: in the temple courts on the Day of Atonement, Yom Kippur, the one day each year when Israel's sins were dealt with as a nation.

Picture the crowd pressed together in the morning sun. The high priest has set aside his golden garments and put on plain white linen. He carries the blood of the sacrifice past the great curtain and disappears into the Most Holy Place, the inner room of God's presence where no one else may ever go. Outside, thousands of people wait in silence. The Mishnah, an early collection of Jewish tradition, records that the high priest kept his prayer inside short so as not to put Israel in terror, because if he lingered, the people began to fear that God had struck him down and their sins remained. Then the curtain moves, the priest steps out alive, and relief rolls through the courts. The sacrifice has been accepted, and they can go home forgiven for another year.

Into that memory the writer speaks of Jesus, calling him "the mediator of a new covenant, that those who are called may receive the promised eternal inheritance" (Hebrews 9:15). Then he makes a move that sounds odd in English and makes perfect sense in Greek. The word for covenant, diathēkē, was also the ordinary word for a last will and testament. A covenant is a binding agreement, and a will is a binding gift, and the writer lets the one word carry both meanings at once.

"In the case of a will, it is necessary to prove the death of the one who made it, because a will is in force only when somebody has died; it never takes effect while the one who made it is living." (Hebrews 9:16–17)

That is why the cross was necessary. Jesus "died as a ransom to set them free from the sins committed under the first covenant" (Hebrews 9:15), and with his death the will came into force. The writer adds that "without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness" (Hebrews 9:22), something every worshiper at Yom Kippur already knew. The old sacrifices had to be repeated year after year, while Jesus "has appeared once for all at the culmination of the ages to do away with sin by the sacrifice of himself" (Hebrews 9:26). His will was signed once, and it stands forever.

At this point the comparison with every human will opens into something wonderful. Dale Schroeder never attended a single graduation he paid for. He never heard a nurse describe her first patient or a teacher talk about her first classroom. That is the sorrow built into every will ever written, since the one who gives is gone when the gift is received. Jesus wrote his will in his own blood and then did what no testator in history has done. He rose from the dead, and he lives to carry out his own will for the people named in it.

Hebrews traces this through his appearances, and the Greek chooses its verbs with care. Looking back, Christ "appeared" (phaneroō, to be made visible) to deal with sin (9:26). In the present, he has entered heaven itself "now to appear for us in God's presence" (9:24), using emphanizō, a word used elsewhere in the New Testament for presenting a case before authorities, much like an advocate standing in court on someone's behalf. Looking ahead, "he will appear a second time, not to bear sin, but to bring salvation to those who are waiting for him" (9:28), and here the verb means to be seen with one's own eyes.

One way to read verse 28 is as a deliberate echo of that Day of Atonement crowd. Israel stood outside the curtain, waiting for the high priest to come back, and his reappearance was the sign that their sins were forgiven. Our High Priest has gone in behind the curtain of heaven, carrying his own blood, and the church today is the waiting crowd. When he steps out again, the matter of sin will already be settled, so he will come to bring his heirs home and to see, face to face, the people he died to bless.

Every other will is read after the giver is gone; this one is carried out by the Giver himself, alive, who has promised to come and see his heirs face to face. Dale's Kids could only thank their benefactor through their stories and their work. We will be able to thank ours in person.

An heir lives differently because of this. Many believers carry their old failures around as though the will had never been opened, still trying to pay off a debt that was cancelled at the cross. Verse 14, just before our passage, says the blood of Christ will "cleanse our consciences from acts that lead to death, so that we may serve the living God" (Hebrews 9:14). When something from your past rises up to accuse you, you are free to answer it with the plain terms of the will: that sin has been paid for, once for all, by the One who died and now lives.

The inheritance also comes with the same gentle request Dale made of his kids. He asked them to pass it on, and many of them have spoken of their careers as a way of doing exactly that. Your inheritance in Christ is eternal and cannot run out, so you can afford to be generous with it. There may be someone in your office or your barangay who has never heard that they, too, can be counted among "those who are called" (9:15), and a shared meal or an honest conversation about your hope may be how the will reaches them.

Before the day gets busy, open your Bible to Hebrews 9:15, and where it says "those who are called," quietly put your own name there. You are an heir of a will that can never be overturned, written by a Testator who is alive and on his way back. Like the crowd in the temple courts, you are waiting outside the curtain, and he has promised to step out and bring salvation to everyone who is waiting for him.

articles.title: The Prophet Who Was Told to Stop Talking
articles.dek: God gave Ezekiel a message for a whole nation, then tied his tongue. His long silence may hold the wisest relational lesson in the book.
articles.quote: When your words become rare and true, the ones you do speak begin to carry the weight of heaven.
articles.body:
In 1816, at the Necker Hospital in Paris, a thirty-five-year-old physician named René Laennec ran into an awkward problem. A young woman had come to him with symptoms of heart disease, and the usual way of examining her, pressing his ear directly against her chest, felt improper for a male doctor with a young female patient. Her build would have muffled the sounds anyway, and tapping on her chest told him very little. Then he remembered something he had seen in the courtyard of the Louvre: children pressing their ears to one end of a long wooden beam while a friend scratched the far end with a pin, the tiny sound arriving clear and strong.

Laennec rolled a quire of paper into a tight tube, placed one end on the woman's chest and the other against his ear, and was astonished. Her heartbeat came through more distinctly than he had ever heard one with his bare ear. Over the next three years he carved wooden versions, catalogued the crackles and murmurs of diseased lungs, and in 1819 published a book that taught the world how to listen to the human body. He called his instrument the stethoscope, from Greek words meaning "to look into the chest." Its secret is almost humble. It is a hollow space that carries sound faithfully and adds nothing of its own.

I thought of Laennec's paper tube while reading one of the strangest moments in the book of Ezekiel, the day God took a gifted young preacher and, of all things, made him go quiet.

Ezekiel was a priest who had been dragged to Babylon in 597 BC along with King Jehoiachin and thousands of Jerusalem's leading families. He lived among the exiles at a settlement called Tel Aviv beside the Kebar River, an irrigation canal in the flat country of southern Mesopotamia. In the fifth year of that exile, when he was about thirty, the age a priest would normally have begun serving in the temple, the heavens opened over him. He saw the blazing glory of God, wheels within wheels, a throne like sapphire, and he heard his call: go to your own people and speak. When the vision lifted, he went back to the exiles and, in his own words, "I sat among them for seven days" (Ezekiel 3:15), stunned and heavy-hearted.

Then God called him out again. "Get up and go out to the plain, and there I will speak to you" (Ezekiel 3:22). Ezekiel went, saw the same overwhelming glory he had seen by the river, and fell on his face. The Spirit lifted him to his feet and gave him instructions that must have made no sense at all to a man who had just been commissioned as a prophet: "Go, shut yourself inside your house" (Ezekiel 3:24). His own people would bind him with ropes so he could not walk among them. And then came the hardest word of all.

"I will make your tongue stick to the roof of your mouth so that you will be silent and unable to rebuke them, for they are a rebellious people. But when I speak to you, I will open your mouth and you shall say to them, 'This is what the Sovereign LORD says.' Whoever will listen let them listen, and whoever will refuse let them refuse." (Ezekiel 3:26–27)

The phrase translated "unable to rebuke them" is fascinating in Hebrew. Literally, God says Ezekiel will not be to them an ish mokiach, "a man who reproves." The word mokiach describes someone who argues a case, corrects, and sets people straight; it is the same word Job reaches for when he longs for an umpire between himself and God: "If only there were someone to mediate between us" (Job 9:33). So one way to read this passage is that God removed from Ezekiel the role of the everyday corrector, the man with an opinion on everything, the neighbor who could always be counted on to tell you where you went wrong. Ezekiel could no longer nag, debate, or add his own commentary. His mouth would open for one purpose only, to say, "This is what the Sovereign LORD says."

Consider what that silence did. In a camp full of grieving, angry exiles, every word Ezekiel spoke now carried an unmistakable signature. Nobody could dismiss it as the priest's personal frustration, because the priest had no personal words left to give. His silence became the hollow tube through which God's voice came through clear. And remarkably, the people came to him. Later chapters describe the elders of Judah sitting in his house, waiting to hear (Ezekiel 8:1; 14:1; 20:1). The man who could not go out and lecture anyone became the man people sought out. Many scholars understand this restraint to have lasted, in some form, for roughly seven years, until the evening before a messenger arrived with news that Jerusalem had fallen. "So my mouth was opened and I was no longer silent" (Ezekiel 33:22).

There is deep human wisdom here, and it reaches into our kitchens and group chats. Most of us are quick to become the mokiach in someone's life. A grown child mentions a struggle and we hear ourselves delivering the lecture before they finish the sentence. A friend shares a hurt and we jump straight to the diagnosis. At family gatherings there is always someone, and sometimes it is us, ready with commentary on a cousin's weight, a sibling's job, or a niece's choice of husband. We mean well, but our words lose their weight because there are so many of them. Proverbs puts it gently: "Sin is not ended by multiplying words, but the prudent hold their tongues" (Proverbs 10:19).

Job's friends offer the same lesson from the other side. When they first arrived, "they sat on the ground with him for seven days and seven nights. No one said a word to him, because they saw how great his suffering was" (Job 2:13). Those seven silent days were the most loving thing they did for him. Their trouble began when they opened their mouths and started explaining his pain. Ezekiel, who had also just sat silent for seven days among hurting people, was kept by God in that posture of restraint for years. James later gathered it into one sentence: "Everyone should be quick to listen, slow to speak and slow to become angry" (James 1:19).

None of this means faithful people should never speak hard truths. Ezekiel spoke some of the most searching words in all of Scripture, and the very next chapters overflow with them. His silence suggests something about timing and source. A word of correction lands best when it comes rarely, comes after long listening, and comes from a place where we have honestly asked God whether it is his word or simply our irritation. Parents know this from experience. The child tunes out the daily stream of reminders, but remembers for decades the one quiet sentence a father spoke after hearing the whole story.

When your words become rare and true, the ones you do speak begin to carry the weight of heaven. That is a gift you can begin practicing today. Think of one person you are tempted to set straight, perhaps a teenager, a spouse, or a coworker who keeps getting it wrong, and in your next conversation with them, hold back the correction and ask a question instead. Listen all the way to the end of their answer. Before you offer advice, pray a short prayer borrowed from Ezekiel's own experience: "Lord, open my mouth only when you have something to say."

Laennec's simple tube changed medicine because it let doctors hear what had always been there, faint and steady, beneath the noise. God may want to make something similar of your life: a quiet, hollow space where the people you love can finally be heard, and where, when the moment is right, his voice comes through clear. You may find, as Ezekiel did, that the people who once tuned you out start knocking on your door.

articles.title: The Hands That Made Me
articles.dek: One morning in 1887, a teacher spelled one word into a blind and deaf child's hand and opened up her whole world. A quiet prayer in Psalm 119 asks God to teach us the same way.
articles.quote: The hands that made you are still teaching you, and they will keep spelling into your open palm until the light comes on.
articles.illustration: Anne Sullivan and Helen Keller's water pump
articles.body:
On a spring morning in 1887, in the small town of Tuscumbia, Alabama, a young teacher led a six-year-old girl out to the pump house behind the family home. The girl was Helen Keller, who had lost her sight and hearing to a fever before she was two. The teacher was Anne Sullivan, twenty years old and half-blind herself, who had spent part of her childhood in a poorhouse in Massachusetts and was only a month into the hardest job of her life. For weeks she had been pressing letters into Helen's palm with her fingers, spelling d-o-l-l and c-a-k-e and m-u-g. Helen copied the shapes back as if it were a clever game, but she had no idea the shapes meant anything at all.

That morning someone was drawing water. Anne held one of Helen's hands under the cold stream, and into the other hand she spelled w-a-t-e-r, slowly at first and then faster. Helen went completely still. Years later she wrote that "somehow the mystery of language was revealed to me," and that "that living word awakened my soul, gave it light, hope, joy, set it free!" She ran around the yard touching everything she could reach and asking its name. By evening she had learned many new words, and she remembered lying in her crib that night and, for the first time, longing for a new day to come.

Any Filipino who has ever had a teacher who refused to give up on them knows this story in their bones. Many of us can still picture the Ma'am who stayed after the bell, who closed her hand over ours on the pencil until the letters finally came out right. At the pump in Tuscumbia, understanding came through touch, as one patient pair of hands kept meeting another until the light broke through. Keep that picture in mind, because the same picture lies behind one of the gentlest prayers in the Psalms.

Psalm 119 is the longest chapter in the Bible, a love song to God's word in 176 verses. It is built as an acrostic: twenty-two stanzas of eight lines each, one stanza for every letter of the Hebrew alphabet, with every line in a stanza beginning with that stanza's letter. We do not know who wrote it, but the writer tells us a good deal about his life. He has been mocked and slandered by proud people (Psalm 119:69, 78), he has known real suffering, and he has decided that God's word is the one thing he will hold onto. Today's stanza belongs to the letter yod, the smallest letter in the Hebrew alphabet. Jesus likely had it in mind when he said that "not the smallest letter, not the least stroke of a pen" would disappear from the Law (Matthew 5:18). Many scholars link the name of the letter to yad, the Hebrew word for hand, and fittingly, the stanza opens with the word yadeka, "your hands."

"Your hands made me and formed me; give me understanding to learn your commands." (Psalm 119:73)

The two halves of the verse are joined by a quiet piece of reasoning. The psalmist moves from being made to being taught, as if to say, "You started this work, so please finish it." The word translated "formed" is the Hebrew kun, which means to establish or set firmly in place. Later in the same psalm the writer uses that very word for the whole created world: "you established the earth, and it endures" (Psalm 119:90). The care God took in setting the earth on its foundations is the care he took with the person praying. That person has been put together on purpose, by hands that know every part of him.

The request itself is just as careful. "Give me understanding" comes from the Hebrew root bin, which carries the idea of discerning, of seeing how things connect. The psalmist already has God's commands; he has been reading them, singing them and memorizing them for a hundred verses or more. What he is asking for is the moment at the pump, when shapes pressed into the palm suddenly become meaning. He wants the inner light to come on, and he trusts that the One who designed his mind knows exactly how to switch it on.

Job once used almost the same image in the depths of his grief: "Your hands shaped me and made me. Will you now turn and destroy me?" (Job 10:8). It is an honest cry, and the Bible keeps it for every sufferer who needs words for that kind of pain. The psalmist takes the same truth in a more hopeful direction. Because God's hands made him, he expects those hands to keep working on him. David prays in a similar way elsewhere: "your love, LORD, endures forever, do not abandon the works of your hands" (Psalm 138:8). Centuries later Paul wrote with settled confidence that "he who began a good work in you will carry it on to completion until the day of Christ Jesus" (Philippians 1:6). Being made by God gives you a claim on his patience as your teacher.

That brings us to the most surprising line in the stanza, just two verses later: "I know, LORD, that your laws are righteous, and that in faithfulness you have afflicted me" (Psalm 119:75). One way to read this is as a student looking back on a hard lesson and recognizing a teacher's love in it. The weeks before the pump house were not gentle ones in the Keller home. Helen kicked and pinched, threw food, and once knocked out one of Anne's front teeth. Anne finally asked the family to let her move with Helen into a small cottage on the property so she could teach her without interruption, and those days were a struggle for both of them. Looking in from outside, someone might have called it harsh. Helen later called the woman who did it "Teacher" for the rest of her life.

The psalmist does not say God enjoys our pain, and he does not pretend his suffering was small. He says that the same faithfulness that formed him was present in the hard season as well. Then he immediately asks for tenderness: "May your unfailing love be my comfort, according to your promise to your servant" (Psalm 119:76). The word for unfailing love is hesed, God's loyal, covenant-keeping kindness, the love that stays. The psalmist holds the difficulty and the comfort together in his hands, and he brings both to God.

Perhaps you are standing at your own pump this week with something pressed into your palm that you cannot read. It might be a diagnosis, a child who has stopped talking to you, a job that ended without warning, or a Bible passage that still feels like shapes without meaning. You may have been faithful in the reading and the praying and still be waiting for understanding. Psalm 119:73 gives you the words to pray. You can begin each morning this week with open hands and say, "Your hands made me and formed me; give me understanding," and then go about your day expecting the One who designed you to teach you in ways you can actually take in.

The prayer also reaches beyond you. In the next verse the psalmist hopes that "those who fear you rejoice when they see me, for I have put my hope in your word" (Psalm 119:74). Helen Keller grew up to write books, earn a university degree and give hope to people with disabilities around the world, and every life she touched traced back to one patient teacher at a water pump. When God gives you understanding, it rarely stays with you alone, because others will see it in you and take heart.

Anne Sullivan spelled into that small hand for weeks with no sign that anything was getting through, and she kept going anyway. God is more patient than the most devoted teacher you ever had. The hands that made you are still teaching you, and they will keep spelling into your open palm until the light comes on. When it does, you may find yourself, like a little girl in Alabama, longing for a new day to come.

articles.title: The Lawyer Who Takes the Poor Man's Case
articles.dek: Proverbs warns us never to crush the weak because they seem to have no one. The surprise is who has already agreed to stand beside them in court.
articles.quote: Every person who seems to have no one to speak for them has the Lord of heaven as their advocate.
articles.illustration: PAO lawyers at provincial Hall of Justice
articles.body:
Go early to almost any Hall of Justice in the provinces and you will find the same quiet line forming before the offices open. A lola in a faded duster holds a brown envelope against her chest, the papers inside soft and creased from being shown to too many people. Beside her sits a young father who lost his job at a construction site, rehearsing under his breath what he plans to say. Nobody in that line can afford a lawyer, and most of them have spent weeks being told, in a dozen polite ways, that there is nothing anyone can do.

Then a door opens, and a public attorney steps out with a folder and calls a name. If you have ever watched it happen, you know the look that crosses a person's face when someone with a law degree sits across from them, reads their papers with care, and says, "Sige po, hawakan ko ang kaso ninyo." I will handle your case. The lola is still poor and the father is still out of work, yet something has shifted, because the other side must now reckon with a trained voice standing in their corner.

That small scene, repeated every working day by the lawyers of the Public Attorney's Office and by volunteer advocates across the country, is one of the most hopeful sights in Filipino public life. It is also remarkably close to a picture that the book of Proverbs painted nearly three thousand years ago.

Proverbs 22:17 marks a turn in the book. The short, two-line sayings of Solomon give way to a new section introduced as "the sayings of the wise," and the teacher promises his student "thirty sayings of counsel and knowledge" (Prov 22:20). Scholars have long observed that this section echoes an older Egyptian teaching text, the Instruction of Amenemope, which also warns against robbing the wretched. Israel's teachers seem to have known the wisdom of their neighbors, and they took that familiar warning and fastened it to the name of the LORD himself. The very first of the thirty sayings reads like this:

"Do not exploit the poor because they are poor and do not crush the needy in court, for the LORD will take up their case and will exact life for life." (Proverbs 22:22–23)

The Hebrew word for "poor" here is dal, a word that describes something thin, weak, or hanging low, like a branch that has lost its strength. The verse literally says, "Do not rob the dal because he is dal." The teacher is naming a very specific temptation. Poor people are easy targets precisely because wronging them seems to cost so little. They cannot hire counsel, they cannot take days off work for hearings, and they rarely have the connections to make noise. A landlord or employer who would never dream of cheating a powerful man can find it strangely easy to shave a little off the wages, the deposit, or the change of someone who will never fight back.

The phrase "in court" is, in the original, "at the gate." In ancient Israel the city gate was where the elders sat to settle disputes; it is where Boaz gathered ten elders to settle Ruth's future in public (Ruth 4:1–2), and it is what Amos meant when he pleaded with Israel to "maintain justice in the courts" (Amos 5:15). To crush the needy at the gate, then, was to take the one place built to protect the weak and turn it into a weapon against them. Anyone who has watched a poor family lose a land dispute because the other party knew the right people will feel the sting of that image.

Verse 23 is where the passage opens up. "The LORD will take up their case" translates a Hebrew phrase, yarib ribam, that could be rendered "he will argue their argument" or "he will plead their lawsuit." The word rib belongs to the courtroom. God is pictured walking into the gate and taking the seat beside the one who came alone. A few verses later the same teacher repeats the warning and adds a name: "Do not move an ancient boundary stone or encroach on the fields of the fatherless, for their Defender is strong; he will take up their case against you" (Prov 23:10–11). That word "Defender" is go'el, the kinsman-redeemer, the family member who was bound by duty to buy back a relative's lost land or rescue them from debt. The man who thinks he is facing a lonely widow is actually facing her nearest Kinsman, and he is strong.

This suggests a way of seeing the poor that changes how we treat them. Every person who seems to have no one to speak for them has the Lord of heaven as their advocate. The tricycle driver you are tempted to haggle down, the kasambahay whose salary you might delay "just this once," the elderly vendor who miscounts your change in your favor: each of them walks around with an unseen Lawyer, and he takes their cases personally. The closing words, "exact life for life," are sobering. God treats the exploitation of the weak as a matter of life and death, because to the person being crushed, it usually is.

Yet this proverb also carries good news for us, and it comes into focus when we read it alongside the rest of Scripture. Sooner or later every one of us stands at the gate as the dal, thin and weak before the justice of a holy God, with nothing in our envelope that could win the case. The prophet Jeremiah, writing in Lamentations, remembered that very moment and wrote, "You, Lord, took up my case; you redeemed my life" (Lam 3:58). The apostle John says the same of Jesus: "if anybody does sin, we have an advocate with the Father," and he names him as "Jesus Christ, the Righteous One" (1 John 2:1). One way to read Proverbs 22:23 in the light of the cross is to see that when the sentence of "life for life" was finally carried out, Jesus offered his own life in place of ours. Paul put it plainly: "though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you through his poverty might become rich" (2 Cor 8:9). Our Defender became one of the poor so that he could take our case from the inside.

People who have been defended in this way are meant to become defenders. The teacher immediately adds a second saying that helps explain how good people drift into crushing others: "Do not make friends with a hot-tempered person, do not associate with one easily angered, or you may learn their ways and get yourself ensnared" (Prov 22:24–25). The word "ensnared" comes from moqesh, a bird trap baited and hidden in the grass. Harshness toward the weak seldom begins with a plan. More often it seeps in from the people around us, from an office culture that shouts at the janitor or a family habit of speaking to helpers as if they were furniture, until one day we find our own voice sharp in the same way.

So it is worth looking honestly at the places where you sit "at the gate" this week. Perhaps you hold a payroll, a set of grades, a barangay form, or the keys to a rented room. Moses told Israel to pay a hired worker "each day before sunset, because they are poor and are counting on it" (Deut 24:15), and that same kindness might look like paying your labandera on the exact day you promised or letting the jeepney driver keep the coins. It might mean speaking up in a meeting for a worker who will not be in the room, or sitting with a neighbor while they fill out papers they do not understand.

And if today you are the one in the line, holding a creased envelope and wondering whether anyone will ever call your name, take heart. The Lord has already stepped through the door with your folder in his hand. He knows your case, he has paid what it costs, and he is strong enough to see it through.
